Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX seeks refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1

At the outset of the hearing, the claimant appeared without counsel. The panel noted that the claimant's former counsel of record withdrew his services on July 6, 2010. The claimant sought an adjournment of 30 days in order to retain and instruct new counsel. The panel inquired as to what efforts the claimant had undertaken to obtain and instruct counsel since July 6, 2010. The claimant replied that he had spoken to two lawyers, but could not remember their full names, neither of whom agreed to represent him. In considering the request for the adjournment, the panel took into account all the factors set out in Rule 48(4).2 The panel noted that the claimant had more than two years to prepare for the hearing. The claimant had more than two months to obtain and instruct new counsel in advance of the present hearing. The claimant, in approaching only two other lawyers, did not demonstrate serious effort to be ready to start the hearing. The panel determined that allowing the application would unreasonably delay the proceedings in all the circumstances of the present case. The panel therefore denied the request for a postponement. The claimant indicated that he would proceed without counsel if the request for postponement were not granted. After denying the request, the panel confirmed with the claimant that he was ready to proceed and the claimant replied in the affirmative. Allegations

The claimant was granted asylum in the USA in XXXXX 2000 on the basis of his alleged Rwandan nationality. He obtained permanent resident status in the USA on that same basis in 2005. In 2008, the US Department of Homeland Security served notice on the claimant to cancel his asylum status, because they had information that led them to believe he was in fact a national of the Republic of Uganda. The claimant received the notice to appear for this proceeding and requested a delay of 90 days for the purpose of gathering evidence. Hearing nothing from the US authorities, he decided to visit a friend in Canada. Subsequent to his arrival, he learned that his asylum status had been cancelled when he failed to appear as convoked. He also received a copy of a notice to appear for a deportation hearing in the USA. He thereupon sought refugee protection in Canada. The claimant alleges that his previous declarations of Rwandan nationality were misrepresentations. The claimant now alleges that, in 1999, he was detained on two occasions by the security services of Uganda, because of his acquaintance with a XXXX in the Ugandan armed forces suspected of being an opponent of the government. He subsequently obtained a US non-immigrant visa and entered the USA in XXXXXX 1999, and applied for asylum in the USA in XXXX, 2000. The Minister's Intervention

The Minister of Public Safety served notice of his intention to intervene in the present hearing by way of documents.3 The Minister's intervention related to the assessment of the credibility of the claimant, in light of information received from the US Department of Homeland Security. Exclusion - Article 1E

Although the Minister's intervention did not address the issue of exclusion, it was included as an issue to be raised at the hearing in the screening form dated April 22, 2010. The panel is satisfied that the claimant had adequate notice that this issue would be raised in the present hearing. Issues and Determination

The panel determines, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has permanent resident status in the USA and is therefore excluded from Refugee Protection. In the alternative, the panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of Canada's protection. In arriving at the decision on inclusion, the determinative issues were the identity and credibility of the claimant. The panel's reasons are as follows: Analysis Exclusion - Article 1E
The Schedule to the IRPA provides in part as follows:

SECTIONS E AND F OF ARTICLE 1 OF THE UNITED NATIONS CONVENTION RELATING TO THE STATUS OF REFUGEES: E. This Convention shall not apply to a person who is recognized by the competent authorities of the country in which he has taken residence as having the rights and obligations which are attached to the possession of the nationality of that country.4

Among the documents seized by the Immigration Officer5 were a US Refugee Travel Document, identifying the bearer as enjoying permanent resident status in the USA, and a US permanent resident card. The card was issued XXXXXX, 2005 and valid to XXXXXX, 2016. The claimant testified that they were both genuine documents and that he had presented them both when he was granted admission as a temporary resident at Pearson Airport on XXXX, 2008.

The panel determines that valid and subsisting permanent resident status in the USA engages section 1E of the Convention. The possession of a permanent resident card creates a rebuttable presumption that the claimant enjoys that status. It is clear from the documentation before the panel that the claimant's grant of asylum was terminated, effective XXXX, 2008.6 This notice did not however address the permanent resident status which followed the initial grant of asylum, some five years later. The claimant testified that he felt he no longer had permanent resident status as of XXXX, 2008. With respect, the panel does not agree. The claimant himself introduced a notice to appear for a deportation hearing scheduled for XXXX, 2008.7 The panel is satisfied that the claimant enjoys permanent resident status in the USA until the competent authority issues a deportation order against him. The claimant declared that he chose not to appear for the deportation hearing because he feared subsequent removal from the USA. In the Minister's disclosure dated June 23, 2010, the US Department of Homeland Security states in part: The individual failed to appear for his termination interview; thereafter his asylum status was terminated. The Asylum Office issued a Notice to Appear (NTA), but there was no information to indicate if any further action was taken.8

The Minister's disclosure confirms the claimant's own evidence that he was the subject of a separate deportation hearing. The panel finds it reasonable to believe that if a deportation order had been made against the claimant at the June 16 hearing, or subsequently, the US authorities would have a record of that deportation and have disclosed it. The panel asked the claimant if he had any evidence that a deportation order had been issued to him and he replied that he had no such evidence.

After considering the whole of the documentary evidence before the panel and the claimant's testimony, the panel is satisfied that he is today still a permanent resident of the USA, on a balance of probabilities. He is therefore subject to Article 1E of the Convention and excluded from refugee protection pursuant to s. 98 of the IRPA. Alternative Determination - Inclusion Identity

At the outset of the hearing, when the claimant was asked to affirm the contents of his Personal Information Form (PIF),9 the claimant declined to do so and testified that the PIF misrepresented the facts. The panel asked the claimant if he had signed the PIF at page 13, and he testified that it was his signature. The panel asked the claimant if he understood that the signature was equivalent to giving evidence under oath, and he replied that he understood this.

The panel proceeded to review the items in the PIF which were untruthful. They included the following items: * the claimant's place of birth; * the claimant's nationality, ethnicity and mother tongue; * the details of the claimant's marital status and family members; * the details of his alleged education and employment in Rwanda; * the alleged arrest by the government of Rwanda; * the details of his alleged residence in Rwanda; * the allegation that his Ugandan passport was improperly obtained; * the whole of his narrative. The panel asked why the claimant had misrepresented this information. The claimant replied that he physically resembles a Rwandan ethnic Tutsi, and that he felt by assuming this nationality he would stand a greater chance of receiving asylum in the USA. He elected to continue maintaining that false identity through his application for permanent residence in the USA, his application for a US refugee travel document, and three years of living in that country as a permanent residence. The claimant testified that he resolved to be truthful in Canada. However, the panel notes that in both his application for protection made to the immigration officer10 and his PIF,11 he maintained his false identity. His change of heart appears to have come about only subsequent to the disclosure of the Minister of June 23, 2010.12

The panel asked the claimant if he had any evidence to corroborate his alleged identity as a citizen of Uganda, and the alleged persecution he suffered in that country and he replied that he did not. The only evidence on these core issues is the claimant's uncorroborated testimony. However, the claimant has demonstrated a significant willingness to misrepresent his identity to officials in both Canada and the USA over a period of eleven years. In the circumstances, the panel gives little weight to the claimant's testimony about his identity and the alleged events in Uganda.

The panel considered the jurisprudence. In the Yip decision, the Federal Court held that the claimant has the fundamental obligation to establish his or her identity on a balance of probabilities.13 In the Kante decision, the Court affirmed that the claimant must come to a hearing with all of the evidence that he or she is able to offer and believes is necessary to prove the claim.14 The claimant introduced no evidence to prove his personal identity or his nationality of Uganda. Rule 715 requires the claimant to document his identity and other elements of his claim. With respect to his newly declared identity and Ugandan nationality the panel finds the claimant has not discharged this burden. The panel does not know who the claimant truly is. Credibility

S. 106 of IRPA requires the panel to take into the account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and, if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation. In light of the analysis above, the panel finds that the claimant has not satisfied this statutory obligation and draws a negative inference on his credibility as a result. Without knowing his true identity, the panel cannot be satisfied that the claimant faces a serious possibility of persecution on Convention grounds. He is not a Convention refugee, accordingly. S. 97 - Danger of Torture and Risk to Life, Cruel and Unusual Treatment or Punishment

There is not sufficient, reliable evidence before the panel to suggest that the claimant faces a danger of torture or that, on a balance of probabilities, he faces a risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. He is not a person in need of protection, accordingly. Conclusion

The panel determines that the claimant is excluded from refugee protection pursuant to s. 98 of the IRPA. In the alternative, the panel determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection and therefore rejects his claim. (signed) 'Michael S.
